summary: This experimental RFC adds an option to TFTP, the simple file-transfer protocol often used for booting devices, so that several clients can receive the same file at once using multicast packets. It saves the server from sending the same data separately to each client.

plainLanguage.summary: A teacher reads a story aloud once to the whole class instead of whispering it to each kid one at a time.

questions: how can many clients download one file at once
what is the master client in tftp multicast
how does tftp multicast handle missing blocks
subtitle: Multiple clients downloading the same file at once using multicast

tldr.problem: TFTP is often used to boot many identical devices, but the standard protocol requires the server to send the same file separately to each client, wasting network bandwidth.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2090 adds a multicast option to TFTP that lets all clients receive the same file on a shared multicast address. One client at a time (the master client) sends acknowledgments; when it finishes, the next client becomes master and requests any blocks it missed.
tldr.outcome: This was experimental and never widely adopted because multicast support is limited in many networks, and simpler alternatives emerged.

today: RFC 2090 is Experimental and has not been widely adopted. Multicast is not reliably available across all networks, limiting the practical use of this option. Modern boot protocols like PXE and HTTP-based methods have become more common.

sections.title: Multicast for TFTP
sections.content:
TFTP (Trivial File Transfer Protocol) is a simple file transfer protocol often used to bootstrap devices like diskless workstations or network equipment. When many identical devices boot at once, the server normally sends the same file to each client separately, duplicating traffic on the network.

RFC 2090 adds a multicast option to TFTP (defined in RFC 1782) that allows multiple clients to receive the same file simultaneously using a single multicast transmission.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of sending the same boot file to each device one by one, the server sends it once using multicast, and all devices receive it together.

sections.title: Requesting and Accepting Multicast
sections.content:
The client initiates multicast by adding a multicast option (with no value) to its TFTP Read Request. If the server supports multicast, it responds with an Option Acknowledgment (OACK) that specifies the multicast address (in IPv4 dotted notation), the port number (RFC 2090 recommends port 1758, tftp-mcast), and a flag indicating whether this client is the master client.

The master client is responsible for sending acknowledgments to the server. When the master client finishes the download, the server promotes the next oldest client to master, allowing it to request any blocks it missed while listening to the multicast stream.
sections.plainLanguage: The server tells each client 'receive from this address and port; if you are the master, send me acknowledgments when you get blocks.'

sections.title: Data Transfer and Handling Missing Blocks
sections.content:
Once the client receives the OACK, it responds with an ACK for block zero (meaning it wants the first block). Data packets are sent to the multicast address. Clients that join mid-transfer can request any block they missed when they become the master client. The server maintains a list of connected clients and tracks which blocks each has received.

If a non-master client sends an ACK out of turn, the server responds with an OACK setting the master flag to zero, telling it to stop sending acknowledgments. Each client must either acknowledge the last block or send an error message when done.
sections.plainLanguage: All clients listen to the same radio station (multicast). When you finish, the server picks the next person to be in charge and send acknowledgments.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility and Network Requirements
sections.content:
RFC 2090 was designed to maintain full backward compatibility. Servers that do not support multicast simply ignore the option and proceed with unicast. The RFC notes that each transfer must use a unique port to distinguish its data packets from other concurrent multicast transfers on the same network.

The multicast option works alongside the blocksize option (RFC 1783) for efficient transfers. However, multicast relies on network infrastructure support, which limited its adoption.
sections.plainLanguage: If your server does not understand multicast, it ignores the request and sends the file the old way, so both old and new systems can work together.
